nodes.characterization_summary: α-Ni(OH)₂ shows positive shift of diffraction peaks due to intercalated water molecules; β-Ni(OH)₂ shows stronger and sharper peaks reflecting high crystallinity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns exhibit different characteristic diffraction peaks of α-Ni(OH)₂ and β-Ni(OH)₂ ... The positive shift of the diffraction peaks for α-Ni(OH)₂ might be ascribed to the intercalated water molecules. The diffraction peaks in the XRD pattern of β-Ni(OH)₂ are stronger and sharper than those of α-Ni(OH)₂, reflecting the highly crystalline nature of β-Ni(OH)₂.

nodes.characterization_summary: α-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs display obvious lamellar structure while β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs show well-defined hexagonal shape at edges.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Different from β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs, the α-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs display an obvious lamellar structure (Fig. 2a, b, e and f).

nodes.characterization_summary: α-Ni(OH)₂ and β-Ni(OH)₂ nanosheets are uniformly and vertically grown on Ni foam surface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The α-Ni(OH)₂ and β-Ni(OH)₂ nanosheets are uniformly and vertically grown on the surface of NF (Fig. S13b and S14b, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: Lattice spacings of 0.232 nm and 0.230 nm correspond to (015) plane of α-Ni(OH)₂ and (002) plane of β-Ni(OH)₂ respectively.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The lattice spacings of 0.232 and 0.230 nm in the high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images are in good agreement with the (015) plane of α-Ni(OH)₂ and the (002) plane of β-Ni(OH)₂, respectively (Fig. 2c and g).

nodes.characterization_summary: α-Ni(OH)₂ shows weak diffraction rings due to poor crystallinity while β-Ni(OH)₂ shows clear diffraction spots.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Due to the poor crystallinity, the diffraction rings of α-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs are relatively weak, while β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs show clear diffraction spots.

properties.description: Selected Area Electron Diffraction pattern labeled (d)

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni 2p peaks at 856 eV (2p₃/₂) and 873.3 eV (2p₁/₂) for Ni²⁺, 875.2 eV for Ni³⁺ from partial oxidation; O 1s at 531.4 eV (lattice oxygen of Ni(OH)₂) and 533.3 eV (surface adsorbed water).
nodes.evidence_snippet: In the Ni 2p XPS spectra (Fig. 2i), the peaks at 856 and 873.3 eV are in line with the Ni 2p₃/₂ and Ni 2p₁/₂ of Ni²⁺, respectively. The peaks at 875.2 eV are the characteristic peaks of Ni³⁺. For the O 1s XPS spectra, the binding energy located at 531.4 and 533.3 eV can be assigned to the lattice oxygen of Ni(OH)₂ and the surface absorbed water molecules, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: After H₂ plasma reduction, metallic Ni diffraction peaks appear while α-Ni(OH)₂ and β-Ni(OH)₂ peaks remain.
nodes.evidence_snippet: After reduction, the diffraction peaks of metallic Ni appear, while the peaks of α-Ni(OH)₂ and β-Ni(OH)₂ can still be observed (Fig. S15, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: Nanosheet array morphologies preserved after reduction but become highly porous and distorted; Ni/β-Ni(OH)₂ more porous than Ni/α-Ni(OH)₂.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The nanosheet array morphologies of both α-Ni(OH)₂ and β-Ni(OH)₂ are well preserved after reduction (Fig. 3a and e), however, the nanosheets become highly porous and distorted.

nodes.characterization_summary: Distinct nanoparticles observed on nanosheet surfaces of both heterostructures.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The TEM images reveal that distinct nanoparticles can be observed on the surface of nanosheets (Fig. 3b and f).

nodes.characterization_summary: Lattice spacing of 0.203 nm confirms Ni nanoparticles on both heterostructures.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The lattice spacing of 0.203 nm in the HRTEM images confirms that these nanoparticles are Ni NPs (Fig. 3c and g).

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM and SAED demonstrate co-existence of Ni and α-Ni(OH)₂/β-Ni(OH)₂ confirming heterostructure formation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Both the HRTEM images and SAED patterns demonstrate the co-existence of Ni and α-Ni(OH)₂/β-Ni(OH)₂ further evidencing the construction of the Ni/Ni(OH)₂ heterostructure.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni 2p XPS shows distinct Ni⁰ signals in both heterostructures; Ni³⁺ disappears after H₂ plasma reduction; Ni²⁺ from remaining Ni(OH)₂; similar Ni²⁺/Ni⁰ atomic ratios; O 1s shows stronger surface water and decreased lattice oxygen.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As exhibited in the Ni 2p XPS spectra, distinct Ni⁰ signals can be observed in both Ni/α-Ni(OH)₂ and Ni/β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs ... In comparison to α-Ni(OH)₂ and β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs, the Ni³⁺ in Ni/α-Ni(OH)₂ and Ni/β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs disappears ... In the O 1s XPS spectra (Fig. 3j), the intensity of the surface absorbed water molecules becomes stronger while the intensity of lattice oxygen decreases obviously.

nodes.characterization_summary: β-Ni(OH)₂ has higher oxygen vacancy concentration than α-Ni(OH)₂; both heterostructures show increased Ov after plasma reduction with Ni/β-Ni(OH)₂ having most.
nodes.evidence_snippet: ESR is performed to investigate the amount of oxygen vacancy (Ov) in the samples. As can be seen in Fig. 3k, the Ov concentration of β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs is more than that of α-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni/β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs show much lower charge-transfer resistance compared to Ni/α-Ni(OH)₂, β-Ni(OH)₂, and α-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ni/β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs exhibit much lower charge-transfer resistance than Ni/α-Ni(OH)₂, β-Ni(OH)₂, and α-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs (Fig. 4c).

nodes.characterization_summary: Double-layer capacitance (Cdl) values: Ni/β-Ni(OH)₂ = 168.5 mF cm⁻²; Ni/α-Ni(OH)₂ = 83.9 mF cm⁻²; β-Ni(OH)₂ = 2.35 mF cm⁻²; α-Ni(OH)₂ = 2.22 mF cm⁻².
nodes.evidence_snippet: The calculated Cdl value of Ni/β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs is determined to be 168.5 mF cm⁻², much higher than that of Ni/α-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs (83.9 mF cm⁻²), β-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs (2.35 mF cm⁻²), and α-Ni(OH)₂ NSAs (2.22 mF cm⁻²).

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ optical emission spectra during H₂ plasma reduction show weak H₂ signals (590-640 nm), strong Hβ (486 nm) and Hα (660 nm) indicating effective H₂ dissociation and formation of highly reductive ionized hydrogen.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In situ optical emission spectra are used to detect the active species generated during the H₂ plasma reduction process (Fig. S16, ESI†). The signals at 590-640 nm corresponding to the H₂ molecules are relatively weak ... The two main signals at 486 and 660 nm can be assigned to Hβ and Hα, respectively.
